title: Same Leader, Different Verdict
text:
In many experiments over the decades, researchers had given people descriptions or recordings of a leader at work and asked them to rate the leader. The trick was that the leader's behavior was identical, and only the leader's sex was varied, for example by changing the name on a written description or by using trained male and female actors.

In 1992 Alice Eagly, Mona Makhijani and Bruce Klonsky combined the results of dozens of these studies in a meta-analysis. Overall, they found a small tendency to evaluate women leaders less favorably than men who behaved in exactly the same way.

The average was small, but the bias was much larger in some circumstances. Women were rated especially unfavorably when they led in an autocratic, directive style, which clashed with expectations that women be warm and collaborative. Men who led in the same autocratic style were not penalized to the same degree. Women were also judged more harshly in roles typically held by men, and when the people doing the rating were men.
lesson: People can judge identical behavior differently depending on who does it. When you evaluate leaders, check whether you would give the same verdict to someone of the other sex.
people: Alice Eagly, Mona Makhijani, Bruce Klonsky
source: Eagly, A. H., Makhijani, M. G., and Klonsky, B. G. (1992). Gender and the evaluation of leaders: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 111(1), 3-22.
place: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA
